props.headline: We have built this before, in your industry
props.subheadline: Eleven verticals, each with its own catalogue rules, pricing logic and definition of “in stock”. We know which ones apply to you before the first call.

props.headline: Eleven verticals we know well enough to skip the discovery call
props.intro: A perfume store and a wholesale fabric supplier both sell products. Almost nothing else about them matches — not the variants, not the pricing rules, not what "in stock" means. Pick yours to see how we build for it.

items.name: Fashion & Apparel
items.note: Colour and size multiply into thousands of variants, and colour is the first filter shoppers touch.

items.name: Beauty & Cosmetics
items.note: Shade is the whole decision, and ingredient lists change by market.

items.name: Fragrances & Perfumes
items.note: You cannot smell a website, so samples carry the discovery load.

items.name: Sports Equipment
items.note: Custom kit is made after the order, so the page promises a date, not a quantity.

items.name: B2B Wholesale
items.note: Price depends on who is logged in and what was agreed offline.

items.name: Jewelry & Accessories
items.note: High value per parcel, and configurators that price a combination rather than a product.

items.name: Health & Wellness
items.note: Revenue lives in the second order, so subscription mechanics matter more than the storefront.

items.name: Home & Decor
items.note: Freight, not parcels. Free shipping here is a way to lose money quietly.

items.name: Transport & Logistics
items.note: Nothing is bought from the page. The job is a quote request detailed enough to price.

items.name: Telecommunications
items.note: Availability is a postcode question before it is a product question.

items.name: Education
items.note: Enrolment is decided over several visits, often by someone who is not the student.

props.headline: The same brief, built two different ways
props.intro: Each pair below looks like one job on a proposal. In the build they diverge early, and the decision that separates them is usually made in the first week.

pairs.subject: A product with options
pairs.leftDetail: Colour and size multiply into hundreds of variants, each needing its own stock count, and shoppers filter by colour before anything else. Get the colour taxonomy wrong and the filter silently returns nothing.
pairs.rightDetail: One scent, three bottle sizes, and a sample that is a different product with different margins. The decision is whether a sample purchase discounts the full bottle later.

pairs.subject: A price
pairs.leftDetail: One number, visible to everyone, occasionally discounted by a coupon. The checkout maths is addition.
pairs.rightDetail: Price depends on who is logged in, how many units they take, and what was agreed on their contract. Nothing is shown until an account is approved.

pairs.subject: Shipping
pairs.leftDetail: Small, light, insured, signature on delivery. Cost barely moves with basket size, so free shipping is safe to offer.
pairs.rightDetail: A sofa ships by freight with a delivery window, a kerbside option, and a return that costs more than the margin. Free shipping here is a way to lose money quietly.

pairs.subject: "In stock"
pairs.leftDetail: Custom kit is made after the order, so stock is really lead time. The page has to promise a date, not a quantity.
pairs.rightDetail: Availability is a postcode question before it is a product question. The wrong answer wastes an engineer visit.
